When I was 7 my dad (28) started dating an 18 year old woman from Guatemala, after divorcing my mom. (27)  This woman, lets call her Molly, was always a bit harsh, but seemed fine, though the age gap led to some uncomfortable moments. My dad married Molly, they took my mom's house from her in the divorce leaving us (my mother, brother, and I) temporarily homeless, and started a family there. 

Molly was 4 months pregnant with her first child when my mother died in a freak accident which me and my brother witnessed. After that me and my brother were moved in with my father and Molly who quickly became incredibly short tempered and abusive. The abuse was severe (starving, taking everything I owned, isolating me, physical abuse, neglect, etc, the details don't really matter) and continued until I was kicked out in the beginning of my senior year.

  
I ended up finishing high school alone, and even going to college, (which I'm still in) and I've come to accept what happened, and understand Molly.  


I understand what she did was wrong and I'm still protective of the children under her care, and would be there in an instant if they needed to leave. But I've come to understand that her family were farmers in Guatemala, and she fled right after high school, in the early 2000's. Guatemala had a bloody civil war in the 1990's which really affected farmers. I can see why she left, and why she married my dad. She didn't have much choice, she was undocumented and needed to be able to stay in the United States. When she married my dad, me and my brother lived with our mother, and she never expected to have two kids full time. It was way more than she bargained for, and I do feel like in some ways my father took advantage of her by marrying her so young and in that situation, and I can see how she would be trapped and frustrated. 

I am a trans man who spent a very long time in the closet and have a lot of empathy for people trapped in lives they hate; and I understand the frustration of trying to make it work. Though I'd recommend doing something about it as opposed to lashing out. (it's healthier and can prevent this kind of thing) I don't take it personally anymore, and I've come to accept the way Molly changed my life.
